title: February minutes show why the RBA reversed course as private demand outgrew capacity
summary: At its meeting on 2–3 February, the Monetary Policy Board unanimously raised the cash rate from 3.60% to 3.85%. The minutes were published on 17 February. The immediate problem was a change in the balance between demand and the economy’s ability to supply it. Staff still thought temporary factors accounted for most of the latest increase in inflation, but the persistent part was large enough to matter. Waiting for every source of price pressure to prove durable would have meant accepting a longer period above the target. Meanwhile, the risk that a modest increase would precipitate a sharp deterioration in employment had diminished (Economic conditions and Considerations for monetary policy).

The breadth of price increases was more telling than any single category. Both headline and underlying measures had exceeded expectations in successive quarters. The share of items rising at an annualised pace above 2.5% had increased sharply and was high relative to its own history. Electricity, travel and groceries could move substantially for transitory reasons. New dwellings and durables faced sector-specific pressures. Administered prices excluding electricity had increased comparatively modestly relative to history. The Board therefore had evidence of important exceptions to its broad reading. What made the diagnosis more persuasive was the simultaneous evidence from capacity surveys, employment and underlying domestic demand. Breadth, in isolation, would not identify the cause of inflation (Economic conditions).

Earlier spending and income data had also been revised. Real disposable income was stronger than previously thought. Promotions likely shifted some consumption into the December quarter, while year-ended growth indicated a more sustained recovery. Private investment surprised to the upside, including spending on data centres. Faster spending raised the level of demand relative to capacity today even if some of that investment could add productive capacity later. Members attributed most of the tightening in capacity to demand, while staff also lowered their assessment of the supply side a little. This combination explained how the inflation forecast could move even with uncertainty about the timing of the consumer recovery (Economic conditions and Outlook).

Business surveys indicated above-average use of capacity. Model estimates had shifted towards excess demand and were now closer to those surveys. Unemployment was lower than expected and underemployment historically low. Unit labour cost growth remained strong, despite gradual slowing in private wage growth. Together these readings suggested the labour market was slightly tighter than consistent with full employment. The judgement involved estimates of sustainable labour utilisation and productive capacity. Neither is observed directly. Realised employment resilience reduced the downside employment risk relevant to the immediate decision, without guaranteeing that tighter borrowing conditions would leave jobs unaffected later (Economic conditions and Considerations for monetary policy).

The staff forecast embodies a sizeable change in its interest-rate assumption. In November it had been conditioned on a decline of about 30 basis points over the forecast period. In February the new market path instead implied an increase of roughly 60 basis points by its end. Even so, output growth was projected to outpace growth in productive capacity during much of 2026. Staff expected underlying trimmed mean inflation to peak at 3.7% around midyear and headline inflation at 4.2%, partly because electricity rebates expired. Both measures fell a little below 3% by mid-2027 and approached a level just above the target midpoint around mid-2028. Projected unemployment drifted from roughly 4¼% to 4½%. Reading those inflation numbers against an unchanged policy rate would silently discard a central input to the projection (Outlook).

Credit prices and quantities complicated the assessment of how restrictive policy already was. Housing credit growth had overtaken income growth, partly through lending to investors. Business debt was expanding faster than GDP and at its fastest pace since the global financial crisis. Narrow capital-market risk premia eased financing for larger borrowers. Yet mortgage payments relative to disposable income remained historically high and households continued adding to offset and redraw accounts. Additional saving could mean rates were restraining expenditure. It could also mean that unexpectedly strong income had temporarily accumulated as liquid balances that households might spend later. The distinction matters to the timing of demand and the sensitivity of mortgagors to the next rate move (Financial conditions).

Market pricing implied about a 70% chance of an increase at the meeting, with another increase fully priced by year-end. On a trade-weighted basis the Australian dollar had risen about 5% since November. A higher currency could lower import prices and restrain net exports. Where that appreciation reflected expectations of domestic rate increases, it was already part of the projected transmission of the market rate path. Adding it as a separate tightening shock would double-count the effect. Higher commodity prices also mattered, so the exchange rate could not be attributed entirely to RBA expectations. Australian equities had underperformed alongside higher expected domestic rates, even as demand for securities issued by Australian companies remained strong (Financial conditions and Outlook).

The Board also considered why credit spreads and equity risk compensation abroad remained low despite geopolitical and institutional uncertainty. Resilient activity, sound private balance sheets and expectations of an official response to a sharp downturn could explain some of the pricing. Markets might also struggle to price events whose probability and timing were unclear. A jump in risk premia from a low starting point could tighten Australian funding conditions without another change in the domestic cash rate (Financial conditions).

The Board tested the hold against a specific alternative account of the data. Temporary price increases would need to unwind promptly, spare capacity would need to be greater than estimated, demand momentum would need to fade, or productivity would need to expand supply relatively quickly. Those developments remained possible. The members found the combined evidence too strong to rely on them, particularly given the length of time inflation had already spent above target. Their unanimous vote reversed some of the earlier easing. It did not establish a sequence of increases. Quicker disinflation, weaker spending or more restrictive financing could change the outlook, while firmer expectations or tighter capacity could make persistence worse. The minutes explain that distribution of risks two weeks after the public decision. A market event study must date these two disclosures separately (Considerations for monetary policy and The decision).

questions.question: Does price breadth signal excess demand after removing the sectors the Board judged unusually volatile?
questions.detail: Track the fraction of items rising faster than 2.5% annualised with consistent basket weights. Construct versions excluding electricity, travel and other identified volatile categories, then compare them with contemporaneous capacity surveys and unit labour costs. Test their ability to predict later broad inflation using the data vintages available in February. A temporary common cost shock can raise breadth even in the absence of strong domestic demand.

questions.question: Were increased mortgage offsets evidence of restraint or delayed household spending?
questions.detail: Compare households with similar debt, required repayments and income but different unexpected income gains. Follow changes in liquid balances, discretionary spending and refinancing over subsequent months. High additional repayments alongside persistent weak consumption support a different interpretation from balances accumulated briefly ahead of a spending rebound. Account for investor housing credit separately from the cash flow of existing owner-occupiers.

questions.question: Which component of the Australian dollar’s appreciation had an independent effect on inflation?
questions.detail: Align currency, commodity-price and rate-differential changes with their respective news times. Estimate import-price pass-through under rate-driven and commodity-driven appreciations, controlling for global prices. Keep the 3 February decision distinct from the 17 February minutes. A broad exchange-rate rise over several months cannot be treated as the currency return caused by either publication.
